title: AI and the tools you will use
source_deliverable: Hello, AI World! - build a simple program that automates a task or makes a decision using logic.
summary: Start from zero: what artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning actually mean, how a program makes a decision, the Python used every day in this course, and how to keep your work in a notebook and on GitHub.
topics: What AI, ML and DL mean
outcomes: Explain the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning in plain words.
Write a decision rule in plain language and implement it as a Python function.
Read and write the Python used in every later module: values, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions.
Run code in a notebook, commit it to Git, and publish it on GitHub.

lessons.title: What AI, machine learning, and deep learning actually mean
lessons.goal: Describe the difference between artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning, and name where each one appears in products you already use.

sections.heading: A program that follows written rules
sections.intent: Start with rule-based software: the computer follows instructions a person wrote, and the same input always gives the same output. Give a concrete example such as a spam filter that blocks any message containing a banned phrase.

sections.heading: A program that learns from examples
sections.intent: Introduce machine learning: instead of writing the rule, you show many labelled examples and the program finds a rule that fits them. Use one everyday example such as a phone unlocking by recognising a face.

sections.heading: Where deep learning fits
sections.intent: Explain deep learning as machine learning that uses many stacked layers of simple numbers to learn features by itself. Keep it concrete: layers of numbers, trained on many examples.

sections.heading: How to tell what a product really uses
sections.intent: Give the learner a checklist for reading product descriptions honestly: is the behaviour a written rule, a learned model, or a deep network? Warn that marketing language is often vague.

lessons.task: Pick one product you use every day. Write three short sentences: the part that works from written rules, the part that learned from examples, and what data each part uses.
quiz: A rule written by a person and a model trained on examples are two different ways to build the same behaviour. What is the key difference between them?
Which of these is an everyday example of deep learning rather than simple rules?
A product claims it uses 'AI'. Which question best helps you check whether it is actually a learned model?

lessons.title: How a program makes a decision
lessons.goal: Write a decision rule in plain language and turn it into a Python function that always returns the same answer for the same input.

sections.heading: Inputs, rules, outputs
sections.intent: Define the three parts of any decision: what you know (inputs), the rule you apply, and the answer you produce (outputs). Use the refund example from the module project.

sections.heading: From a sentence to a table
sections.intent: Show how a written rule such as 'approve damaged orders' becomes a table of conditions and results that a person can check.

sections.heading: Writing the decision in Python
sections.intent: Teach if / elif / else with a worked example, including why the first matching branch wins and why order changes the answer.

sections.heading: Testing the decision
sections.intent: Show why you write down expected answers before coding, then check your function against them. Point out that a decision with no test is just an opinion.

lessons.task: Write a Python function decide(request) that returns 'approve', 'review', or 'decline' for a refund request. Use these rules, and the first one that matches wins: a damaged or wrong item means approve; a late delivery means review; a request that arrived by email means decline; an amount of 50 or more means review; anything else means approve. Test it on four requests.
quiz: Why does the order of the branches matter in an if / elif / else chain?
For a request with amount 80 and reason 'late_delivery', what does the rule set in the lesson return, and why?
Which test would catch the classic beginner mistake of swapping the 'amount >= 50' check with the 'email' check?

lessons.title: Python essentials for this course
lessons.goal: Read and write the Python used every day in this course: values, lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions that return a result.

sections.heading: Values and variables
sections.intent: Introduce variables as labelled boxes, and the basic value types: text (str), whole numbers (int), decimals (float), and true/false (bool). Give a worked example with a refund amount.

sections.heading: Lists and dictionaries
sections.intent: Show a list as an ordered row of values and a dictionary as a labelled record, using one email record as the example. Explain when to use each.

sections.heading: Loops
sections.intent: Teach the for loop over a list, including the loop variable, and mention the common off-by-one and indentation mistakes.

sections.heading: Functions that return a result
sections.intent: Explain a function as a reusable named recipe that takes inputs and returns an output, then show the same three lines of logic written three times and once as a function.

lessons.task: Write a function summarize_rows(rows) that takes a list of dictionaries with 'amount' and 'reason' keys and returns a dictionary with 'count', 'total', and 'approved_count' where amount is 50 or more. Run it on three rows.
quiz: What is the difference between a list and a dictionary in the terms used in this lesson?
What does a function return, and what happens to a value printed inside a function?
A loop over a list of three items runs the body three times. What is the value of the loop variable after the loop finishes?

lessons.title: Your notebook, your repository, your future employer
lessons.goal: Run Python in a notebook, keep every change in Git, and publish the work on GitHub so that another person can run it and check your result.

sections.heading: Notebook cells and why order matters
sections.intent: Explain a notebook cell, that state flows top to bottom, and that a notebook which only works when you click cells in a magic order is broken. Recommend restarting and running all cells.

sections.heading: What Git records
sections.intent: Explain a commit as a named snapshot with a message, a branch as a named line of work, and how the history lets you see what changed and when.

sections.heading: Commit, push, pull
sections.intent: Walk through the everyday loop with the exact commands and what each one does, including the pull that brings in other people's changes.

sections.heading: A repository a stranger can run
sections.intent: Give the four things a reviewer needs: a README that says what the project does and how to run it, pinned dependencies, tests that run with one command, and a licence note for data.

lessons.task: Create a notebook with three cells (imports, a decision function, a call that prints a result), restart it and run all cells from the top, then make two commits with clear messages and push the repository to GitHub.
quiz: What does a Git commit record?
Why should you restart a notebook and run every cell from the top before sharing it?
A reviewer opens your repository and cannot tell how to run it. Which file is missing and what should it contain?

project.brief: Build the 'Hello, AI World!' mini-project: a small Python program that automates a task or makes a decision using clear written logic. Use the bundled support-request dataset, decide on every request with your rules, and prove your decision table works.
deliverables: A public GitHub repository with a README that explains the task, the rules, and the exact command that runs it.
A rules table in src/rules.py with at least three named rules.
A program that records one decision per request in artifacts/decisions.jsonl.
A test file that passes in CI on every push.

rubric.criterion: Rules are written down and implemented exactly as described
The decision program is correct on every bundled request
Repository, README and tests let a stranger run the project

kit.dataset: data/requests.json - 12 support requests with id, channel (web, mobile, email, partner), amount, reason (damaged, wrong_item, late_delivery, other) and the expected decision for the rule set in the lesson.
artifacts: src/rules.py - the learner writes RULES, a list of dicts with keys name, when, then.
src/automation.py - the learner implements decide(request) and run_all().
artifacts/decisions.jsonl - one JSON object per line with id and decision, written by run_all().
